analysis.one_liner: Requires two-person crews, slower speeds, safer tank cars, and defect detectors for trains hauling hazardous materials.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan railroad safety bill with 33 cosponsors — 27 Democrats and 6 Republicans — died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tighten safety rules for trains carrying hazardous materials after a string of high-profile derailments. It requires at least a two-person crew on most Class I freight trains, caps speeds for dangerous trains, speeds up the phase-out of older tank cars in favor of stronger DOT-117 models, mandates wayside defect detector networks with federal performance standards, raises civil penalties for rail safety violations to as much as $5 million for deadly incidents, and requires railroads to share real-time cargo information with first responders. It also funds crossing-elimination grants, close-call reporting, and emergency-communications pilots. The House referred it to two committees and a railroads subcommittee; no vote ever happened before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, drive, or work near freight rail lines — especially communities on routes where trains carry flammable liquids and toxic-by-inhalation cargo. Rail workers gain stronger inspection protections and a crew-size floor. First responders gain real-time electronic train consist information, commodity-flow reports, and a ban on withholding that information during an emergency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Railside communities, rail workers, first responders

how_it_helps.text: Requires Class I freight trains to operate with at least a two-person crew — a certified conductor and a certified engineer — with no exceptions for high-hazard trains or trains 7,500 feet or longer.
Caps all trains at 50 mph and high-hazard flammable-liquid trains at 40 mph in high-threat urban areas unless every tank car meets the stronger DOT-117 standards.
Starting December 31, 2027, bars older tank cars from hauling Class 3 flammable liquids unless they meet or exceed DOT-117, 117P, or 117R specifications.

Requires a rulemaking on defect detector networks, including detectors spaced so any train gets a bearing check before entering urbanized areas of 75,000 or more people, with civil penalties for accidents on routes where a railroad is out of compliance.

Raises rail safety civil penalties to a range of $5,000 to $1,000,000 per violation, up to $5,000,000 for violations causing death, serious illness, or severe injury, with a doubling for repeated or deliberately indifferent violations.

Requires Class I railroads to generate real-time electronic train consist information and share it with fusion centers, and prohibits railroads, employees, or agents from withholding consist information from first responders, emergency officials, and law enforcement during an incident.

Bars railroads from limiting the time employees have to complete railcar, locomotive, or brake inspections and directs audits of whether managers coerce employees into signing off on inspections or repairs.
Establishes a confidential close-call reporting system covering every craft and requires each Class I railroad and Amtrak to enroll for two years.

Increases funding for the Railroad Crossing Elimination grant program to $1.5 billion per year for fiscal years 2025 through 2028 and requires railroads to maintain toll-free lines for reporting blocked grade crossings.

analysis.who_pays: The large Class I freight railroads would bear the direct costs: retrofitting or replacing tank cars, installing defect detectors and telematics, staffing two-person crews, slowing trains, and paying larger fines. Some of those costs would likely reach shippers and consumers through freight rates, and slower, more heavily inspected trains could add days of delay to freight deliveries.
analysis.who_pays_short: Class I freight railroads, then shippers

drawbacks.text: Higher operating costs would not stop at the railroads; railroads could pass them to shippers of chemicals, grain, and other goods, who would likely pass them to consumers through prices.
A blanket 50 mph cap on all trains and two-person crew requirements would slow freight networks and could push some hazardous cargo onto highways, which have their own accident risks.

Sections 121 and 122 authorize $100 million per year plus pilot funding for onboard telematics systems owned by private freight railcar owners — federal money buying equipment the railcar companies keep, targeted only at manufacturers not owned by state enterprises.

The tank car phase-out depends on North American manufacturing and retrofit capacity; the bill itself orders a GAO capacity review and lets the Secretary delay the deadline a year to December 31, 2028 if capacity falls short or interstate commerce is significantly affected.

Many provisions are studies, reviews, and reports — including a two-year National Academy of Sciences study of blocked crossings and multiple Inspector General reviews — so some of the bill's paper footprint would produce information rather than fixes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety gains are concrete and aimed at a known failure mode: trains with dozens of loaded flammable cars, longer and heavier every year, moving through towns with one-person crews, aging tank cars, and sparse defect detectors. The main honest objection is cost and friction — the price lands on railroads and eventually shippers, and the bill does subsidize some private railcar equipment purchases. On balance, the safety mandates and emergency-response requirements are the core of the bill and the subsidies are secondary.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to two committees and then to the Railroads subcommittee on July 12, 2024; neither the subcommittee nor the full committee ever took it up, and the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 with the bill still sitting there.

narrative.text: Representative Troy Nehls (R-TX) introduced the Railroad Safety Enhancement Act of 2024 in the House on July 11, 2024, joined by original cosponsors including Representatives Moulton, Sykes, Deluzio, Van Orden, Rulli, D'Esposito, Stansbury, and Lawler.

The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and, in addition, the Science, Space, and Technology Committee; the next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials.
Thirty-three members cosponsored the bill — 27 Democrats and 6 Republicans.
The bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill dead in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large Class I freight railroads are better off: they avoided two-person crew requirements, speed caps, the DOT-117 tank car phase-out, defect-detector mandates, real-time cargo disclosure to first responders, and civil penalties of up to $5 million per violation for at least another two years.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction — a Republican sponsor with 33 cosponsors split 27 Democrats to 6 Republicans — so its death was not a straight partisan vote; it simply never reached one.

industries.note: The bill imposes the industry's most expensive asks at once: two-person crews, 50 mph speed caps, defect detector networks with federal performance standards, mandatory real-time cargo disclosure to first responders, and civil penalties up to $5 million for deadly violations. These are the same safeguards communities and workers have sought after derailment disasters, so the industry's interest in killing the bill ran against the public's interest in the bill.

industries.industry: Tank car manufacturers and retrofit shops
industries.note: The DOT-117 phase-out for flammable-liquid tank cars beginning December 31, 2027 would generate years of new-build and retrofit work; the bill even funds $5 million for tank car research and orders a GAO study of manufacturing capacity. Meeting the deadline faster would mean the safety benefit the public wants is delivered sooner.

industries.industry: Freight railcar owners and telematics technology suppliers
industries.note: Sections 121 and 122 authorize $100 million per year to install onboard telematics and sensors on privately owned railcars, with priority for cars carrying toxic-by-inhalation and flammable cargo. It is a subsidy to private asset owners, but the equipment targets wheel-bearing and temperature monitoring aimed at preventing derailments.

The AskRail connectivity pilot authorizes $25 million per year for 2025–2028 for satellite, fixed wireless, and space-based coverage so first responders can reach cargo data during rail accidents in dead zones. The money flows to private providers, but for an emergency-response capability.

Shippers of chemicals and fuels would pay higher freight rates as safety costs roll down and face slower transit under speed caps and heavier inspection, but they also benefit from fewer derailments of their own product and clearer emergency-response plans their customers' communities rely on.
